JSON: Name: mcba_islet_autoimmunity Title: Longitudinal targeted metabolomics and strain-resolved metagenomics integrated with in vitro immune assays to identify microbially conjugated bile acid signatures associated with islet autoimmunity in early life Short Hypothesis: In infants, elevated stool levels of primary bile-acid amidates (cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid conjugates) combined with reduced stool levels of secondary bile-acid amidates (deoxycholic acid and ursodeoxycholic acid conjugates) cause increased monocyte pro-inflammatory responses to LPS and a shift of naïve CD4+ differentiation toward Th17 versus iTreg, thereby increasing the probability of islet autoantibody seroconversion within 36 months. Related Work: Human and microbial bile acid metabolism studies have shown that gut microbes transform primary host-derived bile acids into diverse secondary bile acids and recently discovered microbially conjugated bile acids (MCBAs). Prior observational work linked systemic bile acid profiles and select microbial metabolites to progression toward islet autoimmunity, and in vitro work demonstrated that some secondary bile acids modulate Th17/Treg differentiation and innate signaling. Culture-based and mass-spectrometry studies have identified bacterial taxa with bile-acid-transforming enzymes, and initial screens have detected MCBA production in limited isolates. Current limitations include sparse longitudinal human infant MCBA trajectory data, incomplete mapping between strain-level microbiome composition and specific MCBA species, limited sample sizes for prospective associations with autoantibody development, lack of integrated predictive models combining stool MCBA and metagenomic data, and scarce causal functional validation connecting specific MCBA species to immune-cell phenotypes in human primary cells. Abstract: Problem: Microbially conjugated bile acids (MCBAs) are newly identified gut-derived metabolites whose early-life dynamics and immunological roles in islet autoimmunity remain unclear. Approach: We propose a longitudinal, integrative pipeline combining targeted LC–MS/MS quantification of stool MCBAs, strain-resolved shotgun metagenomics, culture-based validation of predicted MCBA producers, and functional in vitro immune assays (monocyte LPS signaling and naïve CD4+ Th17/iTreg differentiation). Contribution: The pipeline will (1) define age-dependent MCBA trajectories in infants aged 3–36 months, (2) map MCBA–strain associations at the species/strain level, (3) assess whether MCBA patterns predict progression to islet autoantibody seroconversion, and (4) establish functional links between specific MCBA species and monocyte and T-cell phenotypes. Expected outcome: The integrated approach will deliver validated MCBA biomarkers and mechanistic evidence of MCBA-driven modulation of innate and adaptive immune responses relevant to islet autoimmunity, enabling improved risk stratification and prioritization of specific microbial strains and bile-acid conjugates for downstream causal studies. Experiments: Cohort and samples: longitudinal stool collection at ages 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, and 36 months from N≈74 infants (target n_samples≈303) stratified into three outcome groups matched by HLA risk: P2Ab (multiple islet autoantibodies), P1Ab (single autoantibody), and CTR (autoantibody-negative). Paired metagenomic shotgun sequencing for a subset of samples (n≈110) matched to stool metabolomics. Metabolomics: targeted LC–MS/MS assay quantifying a panel of 110 MCBA species; include internal standards and pooled QC; report peak-area normalized concentrations and presence/absence. Microbiome: strain-resolved taxonomic profiling (MetaPhlAn/strain-level approach) and gene-level functional profiling for bile-acid-transforming enzymes. Culture validation: select 8–12 candidate strains predicted to associate with target MCBAs; incubate monocultures with relevant BA substrates (e.g., UDCA, UDCA-Asn at 100 μM) for 72 h; analyze supernatants by LC–MS/MS for production/degradation of target MCBAs. Innate immune assay: ex vivo whole-blood stimulation from n=6 healthy adult donors; pre-treat with individual MCBA species (50 μM) and unconjugated BA controls; stimulate with Salmonella LPS (1 ng/mL); measure pp38, pERK, IkBa degradation by intracellular flow cytometry at 3, 7, 15, 30, 60 min; compute area-under-curve (AUC) per marker. Adaptive immune assay: isolate cord-blood naïve CD4+CD25- T cells (n≥4 biological donors); culture under Th17 and iTreg polarizing conditions with test compounds at 100 μM; measure IL-17A secretion by ELISA (72 h), intracellular Foxp3 by flow cytometry (72 h), and RORA/RORC expression by qPCR. Statistical analysis: longitudinal modelling using linear mixed-effects models (fixed effects: age, sex, breastfeeding duration, case status; random effect: subject), MaAsLin2 for covariate-adjusted associations, Spearman correlations for MCBA–strain links, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction; significance threshold q<0.05. Predictive models: train logistic classifiers (e.g., elastic net) to predict P2Ab vs CTR using (i) MCBA features only, (ii) microbiome features only, (iii) combined features; evaluate with stratified 5-fold cross-validation reporting ROC AUC, precision, recall; ablation studies: (A) remove age as covariate to quantify age confounding, (B) exclude culture-validated strains from microbiome features to assess contribution of validated producers, (C) compare conjugate-class models (CA-conjugates vs CDCA-conjugates vs DCA/UDCA-conjugates). Experimental controls: vehicle (DMSO), unconjugated BA controls, and pathway inhibitors for innate assays. Report effect sizes (fold change, Cohen’s d), adjusted p-values, Spearman r, and ROC AUC with 95% CI. Risk Factors and Limitations: Analytical limitations: limited sensitivity or ion suppression in targeted LC–MS/MS may yield false negatives for low-abundance MCBAs; isomeric amino-acid conjugates (e.g., Ile/Leu) may not be chromatographically resolved, confounding species-level quantitation; batch effects across longitudinal runs may bias trajectories. Metagenomics limitations: strain-level taxonomic assignment and gene annotation errors can produce false-positive associations; low biomass or uneven sequencing depth reduces power to detect strain associations. Causality limitations: observational longitudinal associations cannot establish in vivo causality between MCBA levels and autoimmunity; in vitro assays may not replicate infant physiology or systemic exposure due to unknown MCBA bioavailability and host pharmacokinetics. Cohort and statistical power: modest cohort size and limited number of P2Ab converters reduce power for multivariable prediction and increase risk of overfitting; demographic, dietary, antibiotic exposure, and geographic confounders may bias associations and limit generalizability. Culture validation limits: many gut strains are uncultivable or alter metabolism in co-culture, so monoculture results may not represent in situ production. Multiple testing: large feature sets (110 MCBAs × many strains/timepoints) increase false-discovery risk even after FDR correction. Ethical/translation limits: inability to measure systemic (blood) MCBA levels in infants in all cohorts restricts inference about peripheral immune exposure.
